**Research note: PostgreSQL identifier length, column count, and connection defaults**

Three limits come up when sizing a new schema and its pool. All three are stated in the current PostgreSQL manual, and I read the relevant pages rather than relying on memory.

**Identifier length.** PostgreSQL uses no more than NAMEDATALEN minus one bytes of any identifier. NAMEDATALEN is a compile-time constant that defaults to 64, so the default maximum identifier length is 63 bytes (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html). The limits appendix lists the same figure, 63 bytes, and notes it can only be raised by recompiling the server (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). Two practical points follow. Longer names are not rejected but silently truncated with a notice, which can cause two long names to collide. The limit is in bytes, not characters, so non-ASCII identifiers run out of room sooner.

**Columns per table.** The limits appendix gives an upper limit of 1,600 columns per table. The same row adds that the real ceiling is further limited by the tuple having to fit on a single page, so wide column types reduce the usable number well below 1,600 (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). Dropped columns still count toward the limit until the table is rewritten, so a table that is churned through many migrations can hit it earlier than its visible column count suggests.

**Default max_connections.** The connection settings documentation states that the default is typically 100 connections, but it may be lower if kernel settings at initdb time cannot support it. The parameter can only be changed at server start, and PostgreSQL allocates shared memory and other resources in proportion to it, so raising it is not free (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html). On a standby, the value must be at least as high as on the primary or queries will be refused.

**Recommendation.** Keep all identifiers comfortably under 63 bytes with a naming convention enforced in migrations, and keep tables far narrower than the 1,600 limit by normalising rather than adding columns. Size the application pool against the server's actual max_connections value, leaving headroom below 100 for superuser and maintenance sessions, and prefer a small pool per instance with a pooler like PgBouncer over raising max_connections.

**Research note: PostgreSQL memory and WAL defaults**

Before changing anything on the fresh install, it helps to know where PostgreSQL starts from. All three values below come from the current official documentation for the server configuration parameters, and all three are deliberately conservative so that a stock install runs on almost any machine.

The first setting is work_mem, which bounds the memory a single query operation such as a sort or hash table may use before it spills to temporary disk files. The documentation states that the default value is four megabytes, written as 4MB (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). Keep in mind that this limit applies per operation, not per session. A complex query with several sorts and hashes running in parallel can consume several multiples of work_mem at once, so raising it should be done with the expected number of concurrent sessions in mind.

The second setting is shared_buffers, which sets the amount of memory the server dedicates to its own buffer cache. The same page says the default is typically 128 megabytes, written as 128MB, but it might be lower if the kernel settings do not support that amount, as determined when initdb runs (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). The documentation also notes that this value is far below what a dedicated database server should use, and that changing it requires a server restart.

The third setting is max_wal_size, which controls how large the write-ahead log is allowed to grow between automatic checkpoints. It is a soft limit, so the WAL can temporarily exceed it under heavy load or when archiving falls behind. The WAL configuration page states plainly that the default is 1 GB (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html). A small max_wal_size forces frequent checkpoints, which increases write amplification and can hurt throughput on busy systems, while a larger value lengthens crash recovery time.

Taken together, the defaults of 4MB for work_mem, 128MB for shared_buffers, and 1GB for max_wal_size describe a server tuned to start reliably rather than to perform well. On a machine with a known amount of RAM dedicated to PostgreSQL, all three are usually among the first values worth revisiting.

**Recommendation.** Start by raising shared_buffers to roughly a quarter of the machine's RAM and max_wal_size to a few gigabytes, then measure checkpoint frequency and cache hit rates before going further. Increase work_mem cautiously and only after estimating peak concurrent operations, since its per-operation nature makes it the easiest of the three to overcommit.

**Research note: analytics side-store next to PostgreSQL, and MERGE on PostgreSQL 15**

You asked three concrete questions before picking DuckDB or SQLite as an analytics side-store and before relying on MERGE in PostgreSQL 15. I checked each against the official documentation today.

**DuckDB memory limit.** DuckDB caps its own memory use with a configuration setting named memory_limit, which the docs also list under the alias max_memory. The default value is 80% of the system's RAM (source: https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/configuration/overview.html). In practice this means a DuckDB process running on the same host as PostgreSQL will, by default, consider most of the machine's memory fair game for hash joins, sorts and aggregations. If the two share a box, you should set the limit explicitly, for example to a fixed number of gigabytes, so DuckDB does not squeeze PostgreSQL's shared buffers and the OS page cache. DuckDB also spills to disk once it reaches the limit, so a lower cap costs speed rather than correctness.

**SQLite maximum database file size.** The SQLite limits page states that a database file may hold at most 4294967294 pages. At the maximum page size of 65536 bytes, that works out to roughly 2.8e14 bytes, which the page describes as 281 terabytes (source: https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html). The same page notes that with the default 4096-byte page size the cap is about 17.5 terabytes. Either figure is far above anything a side-store next to PostgreSQL would reach, so file size is not a differentiator between the two candidates. The real SQLite constraints for analytics are its row-oriented storage, single-writer locking and lack of vectorized execution, not file size.

**MERGE in PostgreSQL.** The PostgreSQL 15.0 release notes, dated 2022-10-13, list "Support for the SQL MERGE command" in the overview of major features. The utility commands section adds that MERGE was introduced "to adjust one table to match another" and describes it as similar to INSERT ... ON CONFLICT but more batch-oriented (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/15.0/). So PostgreSQL 15 is the first major version with MERGE, and your 15 cluster already has it. Note that the 15 implementation does not support RETURNING on MERGE. That arrived in a later major version, so check the 15 reference page before building a pipeline that expects it.

**Recommendation.** Choose DuckDB for the analytics side-store, since it is built for columnar scans and aggregations and can read PostgreSQL tables directly through its postgres extension, but set memory_limit explicitly rather than accepting the 80% default on a shared host. Use MERGE freely on PostgreSQL 15 for upserts into the reporting tables, remembering that RETURNING on MERGE is unavailable in that version.

{"answers": {"1": "80% of RAM", "2": "281 TB (approximately 2.8e14 bytes at 64 KiB page size)", "3": "PostgreSQL 15"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/configuration/overview.html"], "2": ["https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/15.0/"]}}

**Research note: TLS 1.3, DNS label length, and HTTP 418**

**1. TLS 1.3 specification.** TLS 1.3 was originally specified in RFC 8446, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3", published as a Proposed Standard in August 2018. The RFC Editor's info page for RFC 8446 now carries the banner "This RFC is now obsolete" and points to RFC 9846 (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8446). RFC 9846, dated July 2026, has the same title and states in its abstract: "This document specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol" and "This document obsoletes RFC 8446, which specified TLS 1.3." It keeps the protocol version number unchanged and additionally obsoletes RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) and several TLS 1.2-era RFCs (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846.html). For the guideline, cite RFC 9846 as the current specification and mention RFC 8446 as the original, since most existing tooling and documentation still refer to it.

**2. Maximum DNS label length.** RFC 1035, "Domain Names - Implementation and Specification", sets the limit in section 2.3.4 ("Size limits"): "labels 63 octets or less" and "names 255 octets or less". Section 3.1 explains the reason: the label length field is one octet whose top two bits are reserved, so "the remaining six bits of the length field limit the label to 63 octets or less" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035). So a single dot-separated component of a host name may be at most 63 octets, and the whole name is capped at 255 octets on the wire. Note that the limit is in octets, not characters, which matters for internationalised labels encoded as Punycode.

**3. HTTP "I'm a teapot".** Status code 418 is defined in RFC 2324, "Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0)", dated 1 April 1998. Section 2.3.2 reads: "Any attempt to brew coffee with a teapot should result in the error code '418 I'm a teapot'" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324). RFC 2324 is an April Fools' document, not a standards-track HTTP specification. The current HTTP semantics specification, RFC 9110, lists section 15.5.19 as "418 (Unused)" in its table of contents, which reserves the code so it is not reassigned a different meaning (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). I only confirmed the table-of-contents entry, not the body text of that section.

**Recommendation.** The guideline should require TLS 1.3 per RFC 9846 (noting RFC 8446 as its predecessor), enforce a 63-octet limit per label and 255 octets per full name when validating host names, and treat 418 as a reserved, non-standard code that production services must not emit. Where the guideline cites RFCs, link to the rfc-editor.org pages so readers land on the authoritative, obsolescence-annotated versions.

{"answers": {"1": "RFC 9846 (current, July 2026; obsoletes the original RFC 8446)", "2": "63 octets", "3": "418, defined in RFC 2324 (HTCPCP/1.0, 1 April 1998)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846.html", "https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8446"], "2": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035"], "3": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324", "https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html"]}}

**Research note: platform timeouts and defaults for the deploy runbook**

**AWS Lambda invocation timeout.** The maximum timeout you can configure for a single Lambda function invocation is 900 seconds, which is 15 minutes. The official Lambda quotas page lists "Function timeout: 900 seconds (15 minutes)" under function configuration, deployment, and execution quotas, and states these quotas cannot be changed except as noted (source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html). The same page records one exception that matters only if you adopt it: functions running on AWS Lambda Managed Instances allow up to 5,400 seconds (90 minutes) for asynchronous invocations and most event source mapping invocations. Lambda MicroVMs and Lambda Web Functions are separate products with their own quotas and are not the same thing as a standard function invocation. For the runbook, treat 900 seconds as the hard ceiling for the standard function.

**Kubernetes Pod termination grace period.** The default termination grace period is 30 seconds. The Kubernetes Pod Lifecycle documentation states in its termination flow that "The default terminationGracePeriodSeconds setting is 30 seconds" and, in the forced-termination section, that "By default, all deletes are graceful within 30 seconds" (source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/). The period starts when the kubelet sends SIGTERM, and any preStop hook runs inside this window, so a hook that takes most of the 30 seconds leaves little time for the application's own shutdown before SIGKILL. Override it per Pod with the terminationGracePeriodSeconds field in the Pod spec when the service needs longer to drain.

**Docker default bridge subnet.** The default bridge network, attached to the docker0 interface, uses 172.17.0.0/16 by default, with the gateway at 172.17.0.1. Docker's official networking overview does not spell this out as a single sentence. Instead it documents the engine's built-in default address pools, whose first entry is base 172.17.0.0/16 with size 16, and explains that Docker selects subnets from these pools when no subnet is given (source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/). The default bridge is created first, so it takes that first /16. The bridge driver page confirms this in practice: its walkthrough shows containers on the default bridge receiving 172.17.0.2/16 and 172.17.0.3 (source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/). The same list of pools appears verbatim in the Moby engine source, where 172.17.0.0/16 is the first local-scope default network (source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/moby/moby/master/daemon/libnetwork/ipamutils/utils.go). Note that user-defined networks created without a subnet draw from the later pools, starting at 172.18.0.0/16, and that the whole 172.16.0.0/12 range commonly collides with corporate VPNs. The dockerd reference also confirms that docker0 is the default bridge created automatically on install, and that the bip and fixed-cidr daemon options change its address and subnet (source: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/dockerd/).

**Recommendation.** Set the service's graceful-shutdown budget to a single value well under the tightest limit, for example a 20-second drain, and document the Lambda 900-second ceiling and the Kubernetes 30-second default side by side so operators know which one applies where. For local Docker, add a runbook step that checks for 172.17.0.0/16 conflicts with VPN routes and documents the daemon.json bip override as the fix.

{"answers": {"1": "900 seconds (15 minutes)", "2": "30 seconds", "3": "172.17.0.0/16 (gateway 172.17.0.1)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html"], "2": ["https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/"], "3": ["https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/", "https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/", "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/moby/moby/master/daemon/libnetwork/ipamutils/utils.go"]}}

**Research note: test and tooling defaults**

I checked the three defaults you asked about against the official documentation where it exists, and against the kernel changelog wiki for the Rust question. Each claim below is followed by the page I read.

**1. Vitest per-test timeout.** The default per-test timeout in Vitest is 5,000 milliseconds when tests run under Node.js. The same option rises to 15,000 milliseconds when browser mode is enabled. The config page states this exactly: "5_000 in Node.js, 15_000 if browser.enabled is true" (source: https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout). The option is named `testTimeout` and can be set globally in the Vitest config or per test. The general config index page does not repeat the number, so link to the dedicated option page if you cite it in a README (source: https://vitest.dev/config/).

**2. First mainline Linux kernel with Rust support.** Linux 6.1 was the first mainline release to include Rust language support. The Kernel Newbies changelog for that release says: "This release includes initial support for the Rust programming language," and adds that the support "will be improved in later releases" (source: https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1). Press coverage confirms the same version. Phoronix reported the initial Rust infrastructure pull, from Kees Cook and accepted by Linus Torvalds, as part of the 6.1 merge window, and described it as infrastructure only, with no drivers yet. I could not open the Phoronix article itself because the site returned a 403, so treat that as corroboration from the search summary only. The official kernel Rust documentation describes the current state of the support but does not name the first version, so it is not a source for this fact (source: https://docs.kernel.org/rust/index.html). Note that 6.1 is also a long-term support kernel, which makes it a sensible floor for a team tracking Rust in the kernel, though the Rust abstractions have changed a lot since then and most real driver work needs a much newer release.

**3. PostgreSQL statement_timeout default.** The default value of `statement_timeout` is 0, which disables the timeout entirely. The PostgreSQL manual says: "Abort any statement that takes more than the specified amount of time. ... If this value is specified without units, it is taken as milliseconds. A value of zero (the default) disables the timeout" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html). The same entry notes that the timed-out statement is logged when `log_min_error_statement` is at ERROR or lower. Because the default is off, any limit the repository wants must be set explicitly, either in `postgresql.conf`, per role, per database, or per session.

**Recommendation.** Keep Vitest at its 5,000 millisecond default and raise it only on specific slow tests, set a non-zero PostgreSQL statement_timeout for the application role rather than relying on the server default of 0, and treat Linux 6.1 as the historical floor for Rust while targeting a current kernel for any actual Rust driver work. Re-verify these values when the tooling is upgraded, since the Vitest browser-mode default and the kernel Rust story in particular are still moving.

{"answers": {"1": "5000 ms (15000 ms when browser.enabled is true)", "2": "Linux 6.1", "3": "0 (disabled)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout"], "2": ["https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html"]}}
